storm.summary_layperson: Storms with locally heavy downpours are likely to cross the area through the evening, and a Severe Thunderstorm Watch is active until 9 PM — but the Sound's cooler water should take some steam out of the earliest cells before they reach the cove, while anything arriving later won't get that same protection.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Marine layer is strong right now (14°F air–water gap at 4 PM) but erodes fast as the air cools, dropping under the ~5°F protective threshold around 6:51 PM — cells crossing the Sound before then may weaken or run late, but anything arriving after 7 PM hits the cove at full strength.
storm.detail_html:
A Severe Thunderstorm Watch covers the NYC metro, Fairfield County, and the Lower Hudson Valley until 9 PM. NWS's Area Forecast Discussion describes scattered storms developing along sea-breeze boundaries this afternoon, organizing into a broken line that tracks west to east across the region between 6 and 10 PM, with isolated damaging wind gusts and flash flooding the primary hazards. CAM models are showing very high instability regionally (3,000–4,500 J/kg SBCAPE in spots); the local HRRR column over the cove reads a more modest 1,690 J/kg with 30 kt of deep-layer shear — enough for organized, sustained storms but not an automatic punch-through. Radar currently shows five cells 33–43 miles W/NW/WNW of the cove, the strongest returning 57 dBZ.

The cove's own storm modifier is active: Long Island Sound is holding at 74°F against 88°F afternoon air, a 14°F gap that supports a moderate marine stable layer. This gap is a trend, not a fixed shield — the Sound holds its temperature while the air cools into the evening, so the protective gap narrows fast. It's down to about 6°F by 6 PM and crosses the ~5°F threshold where the buffer effectively disappears around 6:51 PM, continuing to fall into negative territory (water warmer than air) overnight.

The nearest closing cell (31.5 mi W, 45 dBZ) is projected to arrive around 6:01 PM (window 5:36–6:46 PM) — just ahead of the collapse, with roughly a 6°F gap still standing, so it may weaken or run late crossing the Sound. The next two cells (37–39 mi NW, up to 57 dBZ) arrive 6:42–6:48 PM with thinner but still-present margins (5.1–5.2°F). A fifth cell (43.5 mi NW, 46 dBZ) isn't due until 7:24 PM — by then the gap has fallen to roughly 2°F, below threshold, so it gets no protective discount and should be treated at full strength.

Net effect: expect the cove to see wind and rain from the early wave with a real chance it arrives lighter or later than the regional picture suggests, while inland Fairfield County likely takes the watch at face value. Anything crossing after about 7 PM should be assumed to hit the cove the same as everywhere else.

What would change this call: faster storm motion (currently measured at 16.4 kt) would pull ETAs earlier into the still-protected window; a jump in local CAPE toward the 3,000+ J/kg the CAMs are hinting at regionally could let cells punch through the marine layer regardless of timing; and any upgrade from watch to warning is a hard trigger to high risk independent of the local modifier.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked cell 32 mi W closing at 16 kt; the marine layer is still holding a ~6°F buffer at arrival, which may weaken it or push it late.

wind.tactics_blurb: No coherent sea breeze today — light, shifty gradient flow gives way to a gusty squall around 8 PM as the evening's storm line crosses the cove, then collapses to near-calm by 10. Stay center and play it live rather than committing to a side.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
The ambient gradient right now is light — the ensemble's authoritative wind average (airport-class stations) is 6.9 kt, and direction agreement across the network is only 0.61, meaning different parts of the region are already pointing different ways. The air–water gap (13.9°F) is large enough to support a sea breeze, but the fetcher's own southerly-fraction and thermal-proxy checks both read false — there's no coherent, thermally-driven onshore flow building at the cove today. Call it a light gradient-wind day with no sea breeze in play (B-light), at least until the approaching storm line takes over as the dominant driver.

With no sea-breeze axis to lean on and a storm line about to run straight through both direction and speed, there's no side of the course worth committing to for the whole window — favor the center and adjust live as the line arrives rather than picking a side up front.

Shift character here is persistent, not oscillating: light and shifty east/east-northeast at the start (Tod's Point shelter keeps it soft), backing toward NNW as the approaching line's outflow starts to organize, then a hard, gusty swing to SW around 8 PM as the gust front crosses the cove, collapsing back to near-calm, variable air behind it by 9–10 PM. That's a one-way, frontal-style progression to ride out, not a shift to play back and forth.

HRRR's surface direction (SE, 133°) and the current western-LIS station ensemble (SSE, 161°) disagree by 28°, but because today isn't a sea-breeze/A–A+ day, the maturation correction that normally reconciles that gap doesn't apply — use the raw HRRR track for the forecast hours and expect it to keep sliding as the storm's own outflow, not a thermal veer, takes over.

What racers will actually feel: 6–8 kt E/NNW through the first two hours is drifter-to-light-one-design racing, finicky and fleet-dependent. Around 8 PM the line's outflow likely pushes sustained wind into the mid-teens gusting into the low-to-mid 20s from the SW — survival mode for smaller boats and a real AP/postponement risk if it's still building at the warning gun. By 9–10 PM it's back to near-calm and variable, effectively done for racing.
